articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China
articles.summary: The storm has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured five people on the Japanese island.
articles.full_text:
Image source, X/Reuters Image caption, 
The islands of Amami and Okinawa are the parts of Japan most affected by the typhoon By Jack Burgess 
- Published 8 August 2026 
Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. 
Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. 
The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. 
Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. 
The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. 
Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. 
Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Satellite imagery showing Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa during the week 
In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. 
A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. 
In Hong Kong, its weather observatory posted a record high temperature of 36.9C on Sunday as Typhoon Dolphin swept warm air over the city. 
Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El Niño year , which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. 
In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. 
Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons – as was the case with Dolphin. 
A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific. 
Image source, Japan Meteorological Agency Image caption, 
The typhoon is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday

articles.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
articles.summary: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Dorje Morup was a keen mountaineer and had climbed many peaks, including Stok Kangri, the highest peak in the Ladakh mountain range By Jehangir Ali BBC News Hindi ,  Reporting from Skurbuchan, Ladakh 
- Published 8 August 2026 
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. 
The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. 
Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. 
Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body. 
They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. 
"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. 
"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" 
Disaster struck on descent 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The body of Indian climber Dorje Morup who died 30 years ago wearing his green mountaineering boots has become a grim marker along the road to Everest's summit 
The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. 
He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. 
"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. 
A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. 
But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." 
Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. 
Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. 
Image caption, 
Morup's wife, Yangskit, says because she never saw his body, she found it difficult to believe he was dead 
Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. 
Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. 
Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. 
Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. 
For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. 
But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. 
Image source, Family handout Image caption, 
Morup's family is proud to show the certificate issued by the Chinese government confirming he had successfully reached the top of Everest 
An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. 
Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. 
"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. 
How difficult will it be to recover the body? 
Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. 
Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. 
"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. 
"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. 
Image caption, 
Some of photos of Morup and a few of his belongings have helped his family keep his memory alive 
The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. 
"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. 
"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." 
Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower. 
Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. 
The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. 
"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." 
"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." 
All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. 
It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. 
But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. 
Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 
'My heart refused to believe he had died' 
For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. 
Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. 
"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. 
"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." 
Image caption, 
Morup's family remains cautious about what the body being returned will mean for them 
Image caption, 
Morup's eldest son, Punchok Dorjai, looks up at a framed photo of his father 
All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. 
If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. 
"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. 
The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." 
Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

articles.title: Perez Hilton faces long recovery after reports he self-harmed during livestream
articles.summary: The US blogger is in a "serious but stable" condition in hospital, according to his family.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Paul Archuleta/Getty Images By Victoria Bourne 
- Published 9 August 2026, 05:32 BST 
The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family. 
Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members of the public reported concerns while watching a TikTok livestream. 
The Miami sheriff's office confirmed they attended a scene of a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm" on Tuesday. They did not confirm his name but said the man was alone in the house at the time. 
A statement released on the 48-year-old's website said he "experienced significant blood loss" and his treatment and recovery would be a "long process". 
- 
If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line . 
The statement , external said Hilton was being held in hospital under Florida's Baker Act, which focuses on providing services for people experiencing a mental health crisis. 
The father-of-three, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, is expected to have surgery in the coming days. 
A TikTok spokesman said its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream to the company's US moderation team for review within minutes. 
A moderator error caused a delay in the removal, TikTok said, but the company alerted law enforcement to the situation, closed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds, and banned the account. 
The pseudonym Perez Hilton is a reference to Paris Hilton, who was at the height of her fame when the celebrity gossip blog was launched in 2005. 
The website would go on to attract eight million hits a day at a time when the internet was still in its relative infancy. It was criticised for vicious commentary of stars including Miley Cyrus and Lady Gaga. 
In later years, Hilton admitted having regrets about being "mean or cruel". 
He has also appeared on reality TV shows including Celebrity Rap Superstar and Celebrity Big Brother.

Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall in China as its strongest storm this year
Tropical cyclone brings torrential rain and high winds to east coast after hitting Japan’s southern Okinawa province 
Typhoon Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hit China this year, has made landfall on the country’s east coast, bringing torrential rain and strong ⁠winds and triggering warnings ​of flooding and landslides. 
The storm has already swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings. 
Dolphin made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province at about ⁠5:30pm (0930 GMT) on Sunday, China’s meteorological authorities said. It brought maximum sustained winds of 94mph (151 km/h) near its centre at landfall, equivalent to a category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale. 
In addition to evacuating at least 30,300 people, Shanghai has cancelled about 1,500 flights, according to the flight-tracking data provider VariFlight. 
View image in fullscreen 
A struggles against high winds and driving rain in Dongsha, Zhejiang province, as Typhoon Dolphin makes landfall. Photograph: Huang Zongzhi/Xinhua/AP 
Authorities moved offshore ⁠workers to safety, ordered vessels back to port and increased checks at reservoirs, mountain streams, landslide-prone areas, construction sites and tourist locations. 
Torrential ​rain is forecast for Monday across Zhejiang, Shanghai, northern Fujian, ‌north-eastern Jiangxi, central and southern Anhui, and ‌much of Jiangsu. Parts of central and eastern Zhejiang could receive 250-500 mm (10-20 inches) of rain, according to forecasters. 
Dolphin was forecast to track ‌westward before slowing over central and south-western China and gradually losing strength, the chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Centre, Wang Haiping, told the state broadcaster CCTV. 
That could prolong heavy rain and increase the risk of flooding and landslides, especially in mountainous areas and along smaller rivers. 
1:12 
Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – video 
Transport was widely disrupted across the east of the country and more than a million people were evacuated from their homes. 
A 42-year-old tourist from Guangdong, surnamed Chen, said he had been stranded in Shanghai ‌after his family’s flight, scheduled to depart on Sunday, was cancelled. 
He said the family had been rebooked on a flight at 10pm on Monday, although they were unsure whether it would be able ​to take off. 
“To us Guangdong people, this typhoon is as ordinary as having a meal and feeling the wind. It’s just part of everyday life,” he said, adding that the storm did not appear particularly strong by the standards of China’s southern coast. 
View image in fullscreen 
A woman wades through floodwater in Shanghai. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters 
In neighbouring Zhejiang province, the city of Wenzhou relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters. In Fujian province, authorities evacuated 98,900 people from high-risk areas, according to Xinhua. 
Fujian maritime authorities ​said 55 coastal passenger ferry routes had been suspended, ​all 115 offshore construction projects halted and 290 construction ​vessels moved to sheltered waters. 
The water resources ministry said the Qiantang, Yong, Jiao and Shuiyang rivers could experience major ​flooding, while smaller rivers in the ‌hardest-hit areas could rise above ​warning levels. 
Authorities issued an alert for the risk of geological disasters in parts of Zhejiang. Residents in areas covered by a red mountain-torrent warning were told to follow local evacuation orders. 
Shanghai’s Yangshan port had cleared ships from its berths and moved more than 500 small and medium-sized vessels to shelter as Dolphin approached, the city’s maritime safety administration said. 
Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.

The US private prison company running Australia’s immigration detention system was warned that a newly detained Chinese citizen expressed suicidal ideation and had a history of self-harm less than 24 hours before she died by suicide in a Melbourne detention centre, internal documents show. 
The death has raised serious questions about whether the detainee was properly monitored and whether she was placed in an appropriate room, given her state of mind. 
It has also triggered an intervention from Australia’s biggest trading partner, Guardian Australia can reveal. Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention network 
Read more 
The Chinese embassy has confirmed it has “lodged solemn representations and expressed grave concern to the Australian side” about the circumstances of the death. 
“China will closely follow the case and safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens,” an embassy spokesperson said. 
China’s public intervention creates a fresh headache for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke , who is already furious about a string of security lapses involving the government’s new immigration contractor, Secure Journeys, a local subsidiary of the US-based prison multinational Management and Training Corporation. 
In May the Guardian revealed that a series of failures had allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised and triggered multiple investigations, one of which warned that MTC’s “minimalist staffing model” was putting workers and detainees at risk. 
Burke took the extraordinary step of hauling in the global president of MTC for a face-to-face dressing down in September 2025, just six months after the company was awarded the $2.3bn onshore immigration detention contract. 
On 10 July Australian Border Force issued a short statement saying a detainee had been found dead in the Melbourne immigration detention centre that morning. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email 
The detainee was a Chinese citizen in her mid-30s who had been picked up the day before for allegedly overstaying an English-language studies visa, internal documents seen by the Guardian show. She had no criminal history. 
The ABF transferred her into the custody of Secure Journeys on the afternoon of 9 July. 
The ABF made clear to Secure Journeys that she had previously attempted self-harm and had “recently thought about self-harm/suicide”, the documents show . 
She was found hanging in her room in the Broadmeadows residential precinct, part of the Melbourne immigration detention centre, early the next morning. 
Victoria police are investigating the death, which they described as non-suspicious. The coroner’s court of Victoria said it had directed police to prepare a brief of evidence. Quick Guide

Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny
Imports this year now account for 14% of the market amid claims vehicles are being dumped in the EU and UK 
Chinese electric car sales have risen across Europe to a record high driven by strong demand and low tariffs in the UK and a surge in buyers in Italy. 
Against a backdrop of claims that Chinese carmakers are “dumping” state-subsidised vehicles in the EU and UK to gain market share, the figures will give impetus to calls for quotas and higher tariffs to protect European manufacturers. 
The share of electric cars sold by Chinese brands rose to 14.2% across western European markets – or one in every seven battery electric vehicles (BEVs) – in the first five months of this year, according to Schmidt Automotive Research. The 171,800 sales represented an increase in market share of nearly five percentage points versus the same period in 2025. 
Brands including BYD, Chery, SAIC and Xpeng have targeted Europe for exports, as the Chinese industry seeks to dominate the global electric vehicle market. This has put traditional European manufacturers under intense pressure when tougher emissions rules are forcing them to increase their own BEV sales. Chart showing how China has increased its market share in electric vehicle sales in Europe from 9.4% to 14.2% 
The increase in European sales comes despite EU tariffs of up to 35.3% for electric cars made by some Chinese manufacturers, on top of the standard 10% import duty. 
The UK is the largest European market for Chinese cars because the government has declined to follow the EU’s lead in imposing extra levies. The UK accounted for a quarter of Chinese BEV sales across the 18 biggest Western European markets. 
Although Italy accounted for a fifth of the total, Schmidt said this was an “anomaly”. One manufacturer, Leapmotor, sent thousands of its cheap T03 electric cars into the country to take advantage of purchase subsidies from the government. The subsidies meant that the T03 was as cheap as €5,000 at one point – far below even the most keenly priced models sold by rivals. 
Chinese manufacturers have sold more than 120 different models in Europe this year – compared with about 100 from European brands. 
However, Matthias Schmidt, the founder of Schmidt research, said China’s share of the BEV market may have peaked, in part because they have shifted some of their focus to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. PHEVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, are not yet subject to EU tariffs. 
“I think they are hitting a wall when it comes to pure electric models,” said Schmidt. “They will prioritise PHEVs over the next 12 months given hybrids are omitted from extra tariffs placed on BEVs only. With that loophole set to close in the next 12 months, they will aim to maximise that gap in the door for as long as possible. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
“Given shipping capacity remains limited, more PHEVs means fewer BEVs, which have likely peaked for now. BEVs will take priority again once local EU production comes online.” 
Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, last month called for that to change. Blume said European PHEVs were uncompetitive against Chinese equivalents. The German newspaper Handelsblatt has reported that the EU is considering extending the levies to PHEVs. 
The figures also showed a rebound in sales for Tesla across Europe. The US carmaker suffered a steep decline in sales last year amid a backlash against chief executive Elon Musk’s alliance with Donald Trump and European far-right political parties. 
Tesla sales rose by 60% year-on-year, helped by an increase in demand for cheaper versions of its Model 3 and Model Y. The Model Y was the bestselling individual model across Europe during the period.

Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country 
I magine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population. 
Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians, Uyghurs and others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see as forced assimilation into a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name. 
The new law has been condemned, though not too loudly, by western governments and more vociferously by rights organisations such as Amnesty International . The death of Lobga Rangzen, a Free Tibet activist who set himself on fire in protest outside the UN in New York last month, briefly drew international attention. But such tragedies are not new. Wholesale repression in Tibet and brutal “re-education” camps in Xinjiang are but two longstanding aspects of Xi’s intensifying nationwide war on dissent, difference and diversity. The law and its harsh penalties, which extend to Chinese citizens based abroad , adds legal weight to existing efforts to enforce his and the party’s will (much the same thing these days) by creating a politically compliant, cowed population that dare not answer back. 
A debilitating fatalism has taken hold in the west about China’s behaviour, whether it involves persecution of minorities, evisceration of democracy in Hong Kong, vindictive prosecutions of pro-democracy activists such as the former Apple Daily publisher Jimmy Lai , or vicious suppression of independent Christian churches and “unapproved” religious groups. It’s as though Xi’s China is now seen as simply too big, too economically powerful and too militarily threatening to influence, let alone contain or control. When China’s internal affairs are the issue, it’s easier to steer clear. Awkwardly balancing trade against security , and culpably silent on human rights, Britain is far from alone among western democracies in failing to articulate a coherent China policy. 
But Xi’s increasingly aggressive, uncompromising policies are not confined to domestic matters. In power for nearly 15 years, Xi, 73, is growing ever more confident and abrasive in pursuit of his international legacy bucket list: establishing China as the dominant global power , relegating the US to second place and making his country the essential hub of a new multipolar security, economic and diplomatic order. His legacy list includes a takeover of Taiwan before he stands down, and unchallenged supremacy across the Asia-Pacific region. It all points one way: to Xi’s coronation as the greatest Chinese leader since Mao Zedong. 
With the 21st party congress approaching, 2027 could be a big year for Xi – and he is already getting his ducks in a row. His dictatorship looks unassailable. Top regime cadres, meeting this week in secretive conclave at the Beidaihe seaside resort in Hebei province, are expected to endorse his redoubled drive to enforce loyalty and discipline in the ranks – the official phrase is “sustained advancement of full and rigorous party self-governance”. The Beidaihe gathering, and another meeting due in October , come amid almost Stalinist purges of senior political and military figures. 
Signs of a more assertive international posture are everywhere. In recent months, China has stoked nationalist tensions with Japan and deliberately provoked the Philippines in disputed areas of the South China Sea. Its intimidation of Taiwan is unceasing. This week, Japan’s latest defence white paper singled out China as presenting “an unprecedented strategic challenge” and warned the threat was moving closer to home. Admiral Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command, fired a broadside at China’s “coercive actions” in pursuit, he said, of regional dominance. 
Xi is now actively challenging the US and the west on several other fronts. China is reportedly planning to provide Iran with up to 400 shoulder-fired missiles and new air defence systems. It is already materially assisting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. And an emboldened Beijing is deploying the sort of trade weapons beloved of Donald Trump. Last year it restricted exports of vital rare earth minerals, to Washington’s great alarm. Only this week, China hit back at Trump’s new tariffs by blocking sales of drone technology . 
Xi’s ever more bullish stance owes much to Trump’s trashing of the post-1945 global order, disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland), and strained relations with traditional allies such as Japan, South Korea and European Nato countries. Many now view the US as an unreliable partner. For China, Trump’s shifting focus away from Asia and towards the western hemisphere is a golden opportunity to be exploited while it lasts. That may be one reason why Xi has taken the unusual step of agreeing to visit Trump in Washington next month, so soon after their May meeting in Beijing. 
The main focus of the summit is expected to be artificial intelligence, amid US worries that it is in danger of losing the AI race . According to Chinese commentators, at least, Trump asked for the meeting after China agreed AI partnerships with 28 countries, mostly from the global south. AI is “probably the biggest thing anybody’s ever seen”, Trump said last month. “Whoever wins that race is probably going to win, period.” By which he presumably means, win the 21st century’s superpower crown. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
The summit is likely to confirm the impression left by the last one : that Xi, outmanoeuvring Trump on Asia-Pacific security and Taiwan, accumulating geopolitical clout, and winning trade and tech wars, is well on the way to fulfilling his ambition of gaining the upper hand over the US. Yet in the end, Xi is still an unelected autocrat, a thug in a suit who relies on force to stay in power. He’s failing to deliver economically and, as in India and elsewhere, young urban Chinese may not tolerate his old-school brand of suffocating authoritarianism indefinitely. Who knows? Perhaps his ethnic unity law may ultimately prove a step too far – as it certainly would in Britain. 
All should be on their guard. Xi, no friend of the west, may be morphing into an outright enemy while all eyes are on Iran , Gaza and Ukraine. Symbolically if not yet physically, a dangerously unconstrained Xi is shutting the door on peaceful coexistence at home and abroad.

Responding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK, Prof Paul H Cleverley advocates shared openness standards, while Dr Claire Jenkins says British AI can offer a distinctive path 
Ambassador Zheng Zeguang rightly celebrates openly released AI models, and the Chinese labs behind Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi have led the way – competition that benefits everyone, especially where models can run on modest hardware in the developing world ( The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together, 30 July ). 
But his claim that openness is a defining feature of China’s AI development deserves scrutiny. Take GeoGPT , the geoscience system from Zhejiang Lab showcased at last month’s World AI Conference as a model of jointly governed open science. It is promoted to countries as open, yet under the model openness framework – endorsed in a recent UN report – it would not qualify as open at all. It releases model weights (built mainly on Alibaba Qwen, whose licences are not Open Source Initiative-compliant), no training data or application source code is released , and its governance committee answers to Zhejiang Lab itself. 
Domain rivals show what fuller openness looks like. The European Space Agency’s Earth Virtual Expert (EVE), also built for the Earth sciences, releases its training and evaluation tooling, while the US non-profit Ai2’s OLMo goes further still, publishing everything needed for reproducibility. 
The distinction matters. A free hosted service is not an open one: GeoGPT’s users route their data through China’s legal jurisdiction, creating real dependency and sovereignty risks. 
None of this is unique to China . The US private-enterprise model raises much the same concerns. That is really the ambassador’s own point extended: no country’s ecosystem is quite as open as its diplomacy suggests. If the UK is to gain from the cooperation he proposes, it should press for shared openness standards like the UN-recommended model openness framework as the basis for any joint work. Honest measurement, not just the language of openness, is where real partnership begins.
Prof Paul H Cleverley 
Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen 
Your article rightly argues that Britain cannot afford to be a passive consumer of AI while the US and China shape the technologies that will define the future. Yet the debate should not be reduced to a geopolitical race. 
The real question is what kind of AI Britain wishes to build. Our greatest strength is not simply our research universities or life-sciences sector, but the NHS, our public institutions and a long tradition of ethical inquiry. These provide an opportunity to develop AI that is trustworthy, transparent and directed towards the public good rather than solely commercial advantage. 
Healthcare illustrates both the promise and the risk. AI can reduce administrative burdens, improve diagnosis and widen access to care. However, public confidence depends on strong governance, meaningful human oversight and assurance that patient data serves citizens rather than corporate or geopolitical interests. Recent work by the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency’s national commission into the regulation of AI in healthcare has highlighted exactly these concerns. 
Britain should resist the temptation to imitate either Silicon Valley’s market dominance or China’s state-led model. Instead, it could offer a distinctive path: AI that combines innovation with democratic accountability, scientific excellence and social justice. That would be a form of leadership worthy of Britain’s traditions – and one that others might choose to follow.
Dr Claire Jenkins 
Wollaton, Nottinghamshire
